summary: Identifies what communication networks must offer to support scientific research. It proposes specific areas for near-term work and some long-term goals. It is an idea paper, and discussion is strongly encouraged.

eli5.summary: Scientists need to share big results across the country. This memo lists what the network should be able to do for them.

questions: what network requirements do scientists have
what did the internet task force on scientific computing want
what is type of service routing
what protocols should scientific networks use
subtitle: What networks need to do for science and engineering research.

tldr.problem: Scientific research increasingly depends on networks to access supercomputers and collaborate, but networks are fragmented across agencies with inconsistent capabilities and service levels.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC catalogs near-term requirements (universal connectivity, standardized protocols, reliable transport) and long-term goals (transparent access to distributed resources, type-of-service routing, knowledge banks), organized by four layers: user functions, network connectivity, end-to-end specifications, and user services.
tldr.outcome: This framework influenced research networking planning for decades and helped establish what capabilities scientists and engineers should expect from a national research network.

facts.label: Endorsed organizations
facts.value: Internet Activities Board (IAB), Internet Research Activities Board (IRAB)

today: RFC 1017 captures the requirements thinking of 1987 and helped guide planning for the national research internet. Many of its goals—universal connectivity, standardized protocols, type-of-service routing, and directory services—became foundational to Internet development. Some long-term visions, like knowledge banks and transparent distributed computing, anticipate modern cloud services.

sections.title: What Scientists Need from Networks
sections.content:
The RFC identifies four broad categories of network requirements. First, scientists need user services: electronic mail, file transfer, remote login, and access to resources like supercomputers and databases. Second, they need reliable network connectivity across many sites with adequate bandwidth and low delay for interactive work.

Third, they require standardized network specifications that allow different systems and protocols to interoperate. Fourth, they depend on supporting user services such as directories, accounting, authentication, and documentation.
sections.eli5: Scientists need to send mail, move files, log into remote computers, and use shared machines like supercomputers. Networks have to be fast, reliable, and work together even if they use different equipment.

sections.title: Near-Term and Long-Term Requirements
sections.content:
Near-term requirements include ubiquitous connectivity—every scientist should be able to reach every resource regardless of which agency funds them. The RFC argues that charging models should not be volume-sensitive, so researchers do not treat networking as a scarce resource.

Applications include multimedia mail, remote instrument control, and bulk data transfer from scientific instruments. The RFC notes that different applications demand different network characteristics: interactive remote login needs low delay, while file transfer prioritizes bandwidth.

Long-term goals envision scientists being able to access resources as if they were in their office, even from home or while traveling. The eventual vision is a global distributed world computer with processing and storage resources transparently available everywhere.
sections.eli5: Right now scientists need basic mail and file transfer everywhere. In the future they should be able to plug in from anywhere and have the same computing environment they use in the office.

sections.title: Network Infrastructure Connectivity
sections.content:
The RFC discusses the underlying connectivity layer: the physical links and switches that move data. Packet switching is the preferred technology because it shares available bandwidth among many simultaneous connections and handles the bursty nature of computer communication.

Key requirements include discipline-based connectivity (networks organized by scientific field, not just funding source), sharing of communication resources across agency networks, and adequate physical expansion of links and switches. The RFC emphasizes that overall network engineering—deciding where to install new links and how to interconnect heterogeneous networks—is often overlooked but critical.

The RFC notes that different applications require different network characteristics (high bandwidth, low delay, high reliability), and the network must support a mix of link types.
sections.eli5: Networks need enough cables and switches to move data around. Scientists in the same field should be able to talk to each other no matter which agency funds them, and networks should be designed so no one part becomes too crowded.

sections.title: Protocols and Service Specifications
sections.content:
The RFC advocates for IP-based interoperability as the foundation, allowing different networks to interconnect using Internet Protocol gateways. Beyond connectivity, end-to-end specifications must address:

Access Control protects networks from unauthorized access via phone lines or public networks. Privacy allows encryption where needed. Accounting tracks network resource consumption for management and auditing. Type-of-service routing optimizes different traffic types—interactive traffic gets low-delay routes, bulk transfers get high-bandwidth routes.

Other requirements include local administration of addresses (to avoid bottlenecks), standardized Remote Procedure Call libraries for distributed computing, improved remote job entry for supercomputer access, and comprehensive network operation and management tools.
sections.eli5: Networks need standard ways for different computers to talk to each other, rules for who can access what, and smart routing that gives interactive users fast response while bulk transfers get more bandwidth.

sections.title: Support Services for Scientists
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that connectivity alone is not enough. Users need directory services (white pages for finding people and hosts, yellow pages for locating resources), information sharing services (bulletin boards, shared file systems, distributed databases), and resource-sharing services (authentication, access control, accounting).

The RFC stresses that charges for network services should not make scientists worry about usage, and documentation must be accessible to users at all skill levels, not just network experts.

Long-term goals include a national knowledge bank where scientific understanding, technical know-how, and datasets are organized and accessible over the network, augmented by expert systems to help scientists use these resources.
sections.eli5: Scientists need to find people and resources easily, share files and data, and get help without worrying about costs or needing to be a computer expert.
